extracted.intended_audience: historians of mathematics, classicists, advanced students of geometry and mathematical historians
extracted.subtask_description: Scholarly analysis of Archimedes’ relation to earlier geometers: the methods he used (proportions, application of areas, geometrical algebra), the prior theorems he relied on, and which properties of conics and solids were already known. Intended as an introductory survey for a critical edition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality of Archimedes' contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: An extraordinarily large proportion of Archimedes’ subject matter represents entirely new discoveries; he was not a compiler or textbook-writer but an originator of new results across geometry, arithmetic, mechanics, hydrostatics and astronomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: his introductions where he explicitly states predecessors’ results and then describes how he extended them; statements where he admits long struggles or errors; comparison with Apollonius and Euclid to show Archimedes’ originality. Use presence/absence of systematic compilation vs novel propositions as a criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of traditional geometrical methods (two main methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: The geometrical algebra used by Greek geometers consists primarily of (1) the theory of proportions and (2) the method of application of areas (as expounded in Euclid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a given result is obtained by proportions or application-of-areas; note that Archimedes employed both but relied more on proportions than Apollonius. Examples: expressing conics by proportions (y^2 = p x form) or via 'applying a rectangle' constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of application of areas (application of rectangles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructional technique: 'apply a rectangle to a given straight line equal to a given area', including variants 'exceeding by a square figure' and (in Euclid/Apollonius) 'falling short by a square'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify instances where Archimedes constructs rectangles equal to given areas or uses 'applied' rectangles to express quadratic relations; note that Archimedes uses the exceeding-by-square form frequently but avoids the falling-short-by-a-square form, instead using algebraically equivalent but more complicated constructions in cases like the ellipse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of proportions and geometrical algebra (composition of ratios)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of Euclid Book V proportions including componendo/dividendo and composition/multiplication of ratios to perform algebraic-like operations on magnitudes (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat manipulations of ratios (reducing ratio orders, composing ratios, bringing to common denominator) as equivalent to algebraic manipulations; examples include reduction of ratios between cubes to ratios of straight lines, summation of geometric series via proportions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of central conics via proportions rather than area-application
rubrics_metrics.description: Archimedes typically expresses fundamental properties of central conics in proportion form (e.g. y^2 : ? = ?), rather than by the method of application of areas used by Apollonius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating Archimedean proofs or reconstructions, prefer checking for proportional statements (e.g. y^2 = p x as a proportion) and note his habitual avoidance of area-equation presentations; this affects how one reconstructs his geometric algebra.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of 'falling short by a square' construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Archimedes does not use the application-of-areas form 'falling short by a square' (which would be natural for the ellipse); instead he uses a more complicated expression to represent the same algebraic relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize Archimedes’ alternative constructions (complex expressions in terms of abscissae) when reproducing proofs of ellipse-related propositions; this is a characteristic anti-pattern to watch for when attributing a construction to Archimedes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of auxiliary fixed lines/points to simplify ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduction of auxiliary fixed lines or points in figures to simplify ratios and 'economise power' for handling complicated proportional relations and eliminations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spot constructions that introduce fixed reference lines/points to reduce multivariable proportional systems to a single equation; examples include introducing lines w, y to reduce a*/b* where a*/b* = c/d down to ratios between straight lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination via proportional relations (algebraic-style elimination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Archimedes obtains several equations (relations among points) and proceeds to eliminate variables using proportion manipulations to reduce the problem to a single equation for one remaining point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reconstructing proofs, trace how Archimedes combines proportional relations ex aequali to eliminate unknowns; examples include manipulation yielding mt + nat + ax ... after eliminating variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of exhaustion lemma used in quadrature/cubature
rubrics_metrics.description: Archimedes cites a lemma: the greater exceeds the less by such a magnitude that, if added continually to itself, it can exceed any given comparable magnitude — underpinning the method of exhaustion (Eudoxus’ invention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the lemma (and Euclid Book X/I equivalences) as the foundational principle for Archimedes’ exhaustion proofs (areas and volumes). Recognize two related lemmas discussed and how Archimedes and Eudoxus employ them in proofs of circles/volumes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eudoxus' volume theorems attributed as prior results
rubrics_metrics.description: Archimedes attributes to Eudoxus: (1) any pyramid is one-third of a prism with same base and equal height; (2) any cone is one-third of a cylinder with same base and equal height.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these as assumed background theorems used by Archimedes in further solid-geometry arguments; when assessing originality, exclude these from Archimedes' original claims but recognize their central role in his deductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euclidean solid-geometry propositions (Book XII) used by Archimedes
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of propositions Archimedes treats as known: e.g. (3) cones of equal height are in ratio of bases; (4) cylinders cut by plane parallel to base are in ratio of axes; (5) cones with same bases and equal height are as cylinders; (6) bases of equal cones reciprocally proportional to heights; (7) cones with diameters of bases in same ratio as axes are in triplicate ratio of diameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the standard Euclidean results Archimedes relies upon; when verifying Archimedean proofs, ensure these are available as premises or previously established lemmas in reconstruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spheres scale as cube (triplicate) of diameters (prior theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier geometers had proved that spheres are to one another in the triplicate ratio of their diameters (i.e., volumes scale as the cube of diameters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes cites this as known (and related to Eudoxus’ work); use it as a ground fact in volume/comparative arguments rather than an Archimedean innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parabola fundamental properties (ascribed to predecessors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Properties quoted as proved in the conics: (a) if PV is diameter and QVq chord parallel to tangent at P then QV = Vq; (b) if tangent at P meets VP produced in T then PV = PT; (c) ratio property PV : PV' = QV' : QV'' for chords parallel to tangent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these three as canonical parabola properties known before Archimedes; they are used as building blocks in Archimedean constructions (e.g., Quadrature of the Parabola).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersecting-chords/tangents rectangle-square property
rubrics_metrics.description: If straight lines from the same point touch a conic and two chords parallel to the respective tangents intersect, then the rectangles under the segments of the chords are as the squares on the parallel tangents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is cited as a general theorem from the Elements of Conics used repeatedly by Archimedes to deduce relations of segments and tangents; check its application in proofs of surface-sections and other conic properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parabola parameter relation (ordinate parameter property)
rubrics_metrics.description: If p is the parameter of principal ordinates, for certain chord/diameter configurations one has relations like QV^2 : QD^2 = D : p y and PV' = p AN, QV^2 = p · PY (properties used in On Conoids and Spheroids, Prop. 3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize Archimedes’ use of the parameter p to express quadratic relations of ordinates; when reconstructing numerical/metric arguments, map geometric lengths to parameter relations as he does.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipse properties assumed from Euclid's conics
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples listed: PN^2 : AN = A'N : P'N^2 : AN' etc., and relations involving products PV'·P'V = AQ'V' etc. (properties derivable from rectangles-of-segments theorem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These ellipse relations are treated as prior knowledge; use them as givens when following Archimedean deductions about conicoids and spheroids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperbola properties assumed from Euclid's conics
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogous hyperbola relations: PN'^2 : AN · A'N = P'N'^2 : AN' ... and PV·P'V' = Q'V' : PV'·P'V etc.; also absence of double-hyperbola conception limited some equalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These hyperbola identities are used in Archimedes’ proofs of sections and properties; be aware of conceptual limits (e.g., Greeks did not treat double hyperbola as a single curve).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rectangular-hyperbola constant product property
rubrics_metrics.description: In a hyperbola, if P is any point and PA, PL are drawn parallel to one asymptote and meet the other, then PK·PL = constant (property known to Menaechmus in rectangular case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this constant-product characterization for hyperbola constructions in Archimedean arguments, especially when deriving invariant relations across points on the curve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subnormal of parabola property (VG = 4·?) as prior assumption
rubrics_metrics.description: The property of the subnormal of the parabola (VG = 4·?) is tacitly assumed in Archimedes’ On Floating Bodies and other treatises and was probably known earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When tracing Archimedes’ fluid mechanics/geometry arguments, allow this subnormal relation as an available tool rather than an innovation to be reproved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonic relations (TP:TP' = PV:P'D and TA:TA' = AN:A'N) possibly known earlier
rubrics_metrics.description: Archimedes may have assumed harmonic-type relations linking tangents, points and ordinates in conics (specific ratios given as likely pre-Archimedean knowledge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these harmonic ratio identities as part of the inherited toolkit for conic-section reasoning when reconstructing proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euclid’s Phaenomena remark on genesis of conics from cones/cylinders
rubrics_metrics.description: Statement: a plane cutting a cone or cylinder not parallel to the base gives an ellipse (a section of an acute-angled cone) similar to the conic produced by the generating cone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this geometrical genesis as background when interpreting Archimedes’ On Conoids and Spheroids propositions about how plane sections relate to generating conics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plane-section properties of second-degree surfaces (paraboloid, hyperboloid, spheroid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Archimedes asserts (Prop. 11 On Conoids and Spheroids): (1) any plane section of a paraboloid parallel to axis is a parabola equal to the generating parabola; (2) any plane section of a hyperboloid parallel to axis is a hyperbola similar to the generating hyperbola; (3) a plane section through the vertex of the enveloping cone of a hyperboloid is a hyperbola not similar to the generating hyperbola; (4) any plane section of a spheroid parallel to the axis is an ellipse similar to the generating ellipse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four claims are 'manifest' according to Archimedes; when verifying sections of surfaces of revolution, check constructions that reduce 3D section problems to plane conic properties via intersecting chord/tangent relations and proportional reasoning. Note the special non-similarity case for hyperboloid sections through the enveloping-cone vertex.
